project.name: Rupa Tarakasi — Cuttack's Silver Filigree
project.goal: Build an immersive, museum-quality digital exhibition about Cuttack Rupa Tarakasi — the craft's own material (drawn silver wire, light, shadow, scale) is the visual language, not decoration borrowed from generic 'Indian heritage' web design.
project.north_star: The silver itself should be the visual effect. Beauty comes from macro photography, negative space, hairline rules, restrained type and physically-plausible motion — never from gradients, glow, glass or ornament.
project.content_rule: All factual/editorial content must be derived only from the six supplied source documents (see source_policy). Do not add unsourced history, artisan biographies, statistics, quotes, product claims, tourism claims, or cultural interpretations. Every factual paragraph in content_inventory below carries an inline [source_key] tag; the developer must keep that mapping intact in the CMS/content layer so every claim stays traceable.
project.design_rule: Avoid AI-slop aesthetics: no excessive gradients, glassmorphism, floating blobs, neon gold, generic Indian-pattern backgrounds, arbitrary 3D objects, excessive rounded cards, fake artisan portraits, stock-looking imagery, or animation for animation's sake. See anti_slop_checklist.
audience: people discovering Tarakasi for the first time
students and researchers (archaeology, craft history, GI law)
potential buyers/collectors seeking provenance and authenticity
project.tone_of_voice: Precise, unhurried, respectful. Write like a craft-documentary narrator or museum catalogue essay — never like a tourism brochure or e-commerce landing page. Short declarative sentences mixed with one longer sentence per section for rhythm. No exclamation marks. No 'Discover the magic of...' constructions.

wiki.label: Wikipedia — Tarakasi
wiki.role: Primary source for process detail, alloy composition, motifs, Odissi ornament names, and the Chandi Medha/Durga Puja scale history with dated installations.

vikaspedia.label: Vikaspedia / Archaeological Survey of India — Cuttack Rupa Tarakasi: The Timeless Silver Filigree Art From the Silver City
vikaspedia.role: Primary source for the 'exact origin is unclear' framing and the 12th-century reference; ASI-hosted, so treated as the most institutionally authoritative voice on the unresolved-origin question.
vikaspedia.note_to_developer: This source page did not fully render at build time (JS-gated content). Content attributed to it below preserves the previously-verified claim (12th-century reference, unclear exact origin). Before launch, a human editor should re-visit the live URL and confirm exact wording, then update this file's 'origin_and_history' claims accordingly.

gac.label: Google Arts & Culture / Dastkari Haat Samiti — Tarakasi: The Making of Silver Filigree
gac.role: Primary source for the step-by-step making process: silver bricks, wire-drawing machine, dies, workshop scale, finishing stages. Documented by photographer Chirodeep Chaudhuri with artisan Ruksar Ali for Dastkari Haat Samiti.

virasat.label: Virasat-E-Hind Foundation — Tarakasi Art: On the Brink of Survival
virasat.role: Primary source for the Persia-via-Indonesia maritime-trade origin theory, Mughal-era patronage, the Madhusudan Das / Utkal Arts Work Factory and 1962 Kalinga Filigree Cooperative Society revival history, the rose-motif detail, the '90 types of wire designs' figure, and the living-craft survival challenges.

drishti.label: Drishti IAS — GI Tag to Cuttack Rupa Tarakasi
drishti.role: Primary source for the GI recognition date, the legal/regulatory explainer (DPIIT, GI Act 1999, TRIPS), and the ancient Mesopotamian filigree lineage (3500 BCE).

oaklores.label: Oak Lores — Tales in Twisted Silver: A Tribute to Odisha's Filigree Craft (Sanket Kumar Mahana)
oaklores.role: Primary source for the mid-16th-century/Bhoi-dynasty dating, the 'Silver City' epithet, Bali Yatra connection, named Cuttack market neighbourhoods, and contemporary-craft/fashion-revival notes.

source_policy.editorial_conflict_rule: Where sources disagree — especially on dating — do not silently merge them into one confident timeline. Use attributive language: 'Vikaspedia/ASI notes...', 'the Virasat-E-Hind account places it at roughly 500 years, tracing a Persian route...', 'Oak Lores dates the craft's Cuttack presence to the mid-16th-century Bhoi dynasty...'. The site should make the plurality of accounts itself part of the story — this is honest heritage journalism, not a wiki infobox.
source_policy.copyright_rule: All website copy must be original paraphrase in the site's own editorial voice. Do not reproduce verbatim sentences from any source beyond short, clearly quoted fragments (under ~15 words) with attribution. The content_inventory text below is written as ready-to-adapt paraphrase, not final copy — a copywriter should still pass over it for voice, but the facts and their source tags must not change.
source_policy.media_rule: Use only media the project holds rights/licence to, or that is explicitly reusable. Source citation does not grant image rights. Do not scrape images from the six source pages. See media_and_asset_manifest.

identity.title: Tarakasi
identity.meaning_note: The common gloss offered across sources is 'tara' (wire) and 'kasi' (design/engraving) — present this as the traditional etymology, not a settled linguistic fact.
identity.one_line_definition: A silver filigree tradition native to Cuttack, Odisha, in which pure silver is drawn into hair-fine wire and hand-shaped into ornament.
identity.epithet: Cuttack is known as the 'Silver City of Odisha' because of this craft. [oaklores]

claims.text: Historians trace silver filigree work in Cuttack to the mid-16th century, during the reign of the Bhoi dynasty.

Persian artisans connected to the Mughal empire are described as bringing intricate wire-design expertise into Odisha; native artisans are said to have acculturated these techniques, folding in temple iconography, local mythology and folklore.
A separate account describes the craft reaching Cuttack roughly 500 years ago, possibly by sea — from Persia, by way of Indonesia, through maritime trade.
Wikipedia's material independently describes the art as 'more than 500 years old', practised historically by artisans along Odisha's eastern shores.
Vikaspedia — hosted by the Archaeological Survey of India — notes that Tarakasi's exact origin in Cuttack is not settled, and records the craft's presence as far back as the 12th century.
Filigree as a technique is far older than its Cuttack chapter: Drishti IAS traces ornamental fine-wire work to ancient Mesopotamia, with evidence of filigree jewellery from as early as 3500 BCE.
The Mughal era is described across sources as a period of royal patronage that strengthened Cuttack's reputation for delicate silverwork.
A 19th-century documentary trace exists: an Archaeological Survey of India photograph from around 1873 shows Tarakasi artisans at work in Cuttack.
The early 20th century saw a decline in the craft. Madhusudan Das — described as an architect of modern Odisha — founded the Utkal Arts Work Factory to help revive it.
In 1962, Chief Minister Biju Patnaik established the Kalinga Filigree Cooperative Society to support local Tarakasi artisans.
In March 2024, Cuttack Rupa Tarakasi received Geographical Indication (GI) recognition.

origin_and_history.design: Do not render this as one confident date-line. Build it as a small set of parallel 'accounts' — Bhoi-dynasty/16th-century, ~500-years/maritime-Persia, 12th-century/origin-unclear, Mesopotamian-deep-lineage — each explicitly source-tagged, converging only at documented, undisputed anchors: the 1873 ASI photograph, the early-20th-century decline and Madhusudan Das revival, 1962 cooperative, 2024 GI.
origin_and_history.narrative_frame: 'A Craft With Many Beginnings' — treat the disagreement between sources as evidence of how old and how orally-transmitted the tradition is, not as a flaw to paper over.

sequence_narrative.detail: Silver arrives as bricks/lumps, historically sourced from trading centres such as Kolkata and Mumbai.
A silver lump is placed in a small clay pot set within a bucket of hot coals; the fire is regulated by a hand-cranked bellows. Melting takes roughly ten minutes.
Molten silver is poured into a rod-shaped mould, then cooled in water.
The cooled rod is pressed and pulled into long, thin wire using a wire-drawing machine — historically a two-man hand process — producing 'flat wires' as a base form.

Thicker wires are burned/drawn down further to produce finer wire; gauge is chosen according to the design, and the finest wire can be extremely delicate — by one account, thinner than a strand of hair.

Wire is hand-carved into pattern, or softened over a kerosene flame directed through a mouth-held blow-tube, then strung, twisted and shaped by hand and basic tools — needles for twisting, dies for shaping. Dies produce small circular forms and fine dotted detail.
Across the craft, an estimated 90 types of wire design exist — spirals, curls, creepers, jaali-like lattices — the alphabet from which every motif is built.
A hand-drawn sketch guides the piece. A thicker wire is bent into the outer frame, or farma; thinner wires are then curled and packed inward to build interior detail.
Individual wire elements are assembled into the final composition; for larger pieces, flat cut silver shapes supplement the wirework.

The assembled piece is set in a mixture of borax powder and water, soldering powder is sprinkled over the joins, and heat is applied to fuse the piece — while the metal is still warm it is shaped into its final ornament form.
Beyond core wirework, artisans also practise granulation, snow-glazing, casting, platinum polishing and silver-brass fusion.
The finished piece is immersed briefly in a dilute acid solution to clean it.
A polishing solution is applied, then the piece is hand-polished to a perfect shine using brass-tipped tools and brushes — or, alternatively, oxidised for an antique finish.

workshop_realities.text: Teams of four to five artisans typically collaborate on a piece; workshops are often small, cramped spaces behind showrooms or inside artisans' homes.
Winter months are the preferred working season.
A complex piece can take two to three weeks to complete depending on intricacy, and a single mistake can undo days of work — the craft demands sustained precision.

making.interaction: A single continuous fine silver line travels down the page as the user scrolls, physically bending and coiling into each successive process-stage illustration — melt, cast, draw, twist, frame, fill, fuse, clean, polish — so the 'wire' itself performs the narrative rather than a generic progress bar.

motifs_and_subjects.motif: Animals, birds, flowers, vines/creepers, geometric lattice (jaali)
Konark Chakra (the Sun Temple's stone wheel) and temple mementoes
Scenes from the Mahabharata — most notably the Bhagavad Gita's chariot of Arjuna with Krishna
Lord Jagannath, Subhadra and Balabhadra, and other temple/architectural elements
Non-Odishan landmark replicas — the Taj Mahal, the Eiffel Tower — made as souvenirs
Sun-wheel designs referencing the Konark Sun Temple

specific_design_detail.text: One rose motif — a recurring subject in Tarakasi work — takes roughly three to four hours of continuous work to complete.
specific_design_detail.presentation_note: Present as this source's specific account of one motif's labour cost, not as a universal benchmark for all Tarakasi work.

odissi.content: Tarakasi jewellery forms the traditional ornament set of Odissi dance costume, worn from head to waist. Natural, uncut stones are sometimes set within silver-and-gold work for these pieces.
odissi.visual_direction: Museum-catalogue treatment: neutral backdrop, close crop, generous negative space, labels that behave like object-identification tags in a real exhibition case — never a fashion-editorial mood board.

durga_puja.content: Tarakasi is central to Cuttack's Durga Puja — most visibly in the immense silver backdrops known as Chandi Medha, which frame the goddess's idol, alongside silver crowns and ornaments made for the occasion.

tradition_root.text: The Sharadiya Utsav puja tradition in this form is linked to a 16th-century visit by Chaitanya Mahaprabhu, with consecration historically conducted at the Binod Behari Devi Mandap.

scale_and_labour.text: More than 150 filigree artisans are engaged each year making the backdrop and ornament designs for Cuttack's Durga Puja.

chandi_medha_history.detail: First large chandi medha installed, weighing 250 kg.
Puja mandap installed a 350 kg backdrop.
Committee remodelled its backdrop using 450 kg of silver.

bali_yatra_note.text: Tarakasi work is also associated with Cuttack's Bali Yatra (Sand Festival) celebrations.

durga_puja.visual_direction: Scale contrast is the point: a hairline of wire beside hundreds of kilograms of assembled silver. Use a real macro-to-panorama transition, not an abstract number counter.

cuttack.content: Cuttack has been a commercial hub on Odisha's eastern coast since the early medieval period, and its silverwork earned it the epithet 'Silver City of Odisha'.

market_neighbourhoods.text: Tarakasi is sold and worked across neighbourhoods including Nayasadak, Balu Bazaar and Mangalabag, where hundreds of shops carry the craft.

cultural_role.text: Across India, silver filigree carries associations with purity and ritual — used in ceremonial and auspicious occasions, in royal households historically, in temple ritual objects, and in festival processions.

gi.content: Cuttack Rupa Tarakasi received Geographical Indication (GI) recognition on 15 March 2024.
gi.explanation: A GI tag identifies a product as originating from a specific geographic region and legally restricts use of that name to authorised producers from that place; once registered, protection lasts ten years.
gi.regulator: In India, GI registration is administered by the Department for Promotion of Industry and Internal Trade (DPIIT) under the Geographical Indications of Goods (Registration and Protection) Act, 1999 — itself aligned with the WTO's TRIPS agreement.
gi.context: Cuttack Rupa Tarakasi's GI recognition was granted alongside GI tags for Banglar Muslin (West Bengal), Narasapur Crochet Lace (Andhra Pradesh) and Kutch Rogan Craft (Gujarat) around the same period.
gi.source_note: Use only the Drishti IAS source for the GI date and legal explainer; do not introduce further legal claims beyond what is documented here.

themes.text: The craft is intensely labour-intensive: complex pieces can take two to three weeks, and precision leaves no margin — a single mistake can undo days of work.
Raw material costs are rising sharply as silver prices climb.

Cuttack's artisans face competition from Kolkata, which produces coarser, cheaper machine-assisted filigree at volume — factory processes can replicate thousands of pieces a day, undercutting hand work on price.
Interest among younger generations is declining, given the skill, patience and modest returns the craft currently offers.
Approximately 400 artisans are estimated to still be working in Cuttack; the craft is described as being in real danger of erosion without continued support.

On the positive side, designers are increasingly bringing Tarakasi into fashion shows, luxury collections and international exhibitions, and handicraft training centres are offering renewed institutional support.

living_craft_and_challenges.tone: Lead with expertise and mastery, not pity. State the structural pressures — price, competition, generational transmission — as facts an informed reader should understand, then close the section on the documented signs of renewed interest, ending the site's difficult chapter on continuity rather than loss.

sections.title: Tarakasi
sections.subtitle: Silver, drawn into wire. Wire, shaped into a city's memory.
sections.purpose: Immediate emotional introduction without sounding like marketing copy.
sections.visual: Extreme macro photograph or slow-motion video of real filigree wire catching directional light, shallow depth of field. The object stays sharp; the environment stays dark and quiet.
sections.motion: A very slow camera drift (60–90s loop) or parallax under 20px. No kinetic headline effects, no typewriter text, no particle systems.
sections.epigraph_option: Consider a single small kicker line above the title: 'Cuttack, Odisha — the Silver City' [oaklores], set in the micro type, understated, not competing with the wordmark.

sections.title: The Silver City
sections.purpose: Establish Cuttack and Tarakasi as a living craft tradition, not a museum relic.
sections.layout: Full-width editorial text column (reading_width) with one large image of Cuttack/the craft and a small SourceNote.
sections.copy_seed: Cuttack has stood as a trading city on Odisha's eastern coast since the early medieval period. Somewhere inside that long commercial history, silver was drawn into wire, and the wire was given a name it still carries: Tarakasi. [oaklores]

sections.title: What Is Tarakasi?
sections.purpose: Plain-language definition plus close-up visual evidence and the etymology.
sections.layout: Split 45/55 desktop (text/image); stacked mobile, image first.
sections.copy_seed: Tara, wire. Kasi, design. Tarakasi is Cuttack's tradition of pulling silver — usually 90% pure or finer [wiki] — into threads thinner than a hair [oaklores], then coiling those threads into pattern by hand.
sections.interaction: Hover (desktop) / tap (mobile) reveals a magnified inset of real wire detail — an optical loupe effect, not a lightbox modal.

sections.title: A Craft With Many Beginnings
sections.purpose: Present the differing historical accounts honestly, letting the disagreement itself communicate the craft's age and oral-transmission nature.
sections.layout: Editorial vertical timeline (desktop: alternating left/right; mobile: single left rail), each entry explicitly source-labelled.

milestones.text: Filigree as a technique is already old by the time it reaches India — evidence of fine-wire jewellery exists from ancient Mesopotamia.
Vikaspedia/ASI records silver-working traditions in the Cuttack region reaching back this far, while noting the craft's exact local origin is unclear.
Historians trace organised silver filigree work in Cuttack to the Bhoi dynasty.
A separate account places the craft's arrival by sea, from Persia via Indonesia.
Royal patronage strengthens Cuttack's reputation for fine silverwork.
An Archaeological Survey of India photograph documents Tarakasi artisans at work in Cuttack — the craft's earliest visual record in these sources.
The craft declines; Madhusudan Das founds the Utkal Arts Work Factory to revive it.
Chief Minister Biju Patnaik establishes the Kalinga Filigree Cooperative Society.
Cuttack Rupa Tarakasi receives Geographical Indication recognition.

sections.design: Do not present this as a single confident line. Use a visibly forked/braided rail for the pre-16th-century entries to signal 'multiple accounts', converging into a single confirmed thread from the 1873 photograph onward.

sections.title: From Silver to Filigree
sections.purpose: The signature experiential section — the process, told with the material's own logic.
sections.layout: Scroll-driven process narrative, one wire-path animation running the full section length.
sections.step_source_map: See content_inventory.making.sequence_narrative for the exact copy and source tag per step — pass this array directly into the ProcessStepper component's content model.
sections.interaction: A fine silver line travels through each stage; each stage reveals a real process photograph (or, if unavailable, a specification placeholder — see media_and_asset_manifest) and 1–2 sentences of sourced explanation.
sections.workshop_aside: Include a small aside card using the workshop_realities facts (team of four-to-five, winter working season, weeks-long timelines) to humanise the sequence without inventing an individual artisan's story.
sections.mobile_behavior: Convert scroll choreography into a vertical stepper with scroll-snap; the wire line becomes a simple vertical rail. No horizontal scrolling.

sections.title: A Language of Wire
sections.purpose: Explain that varying wire gauge plus a repertoire of roughly 90 wire-design types [virasat] — spirals, curls, creepers, jaali — form the entire visual vocabulary of the craft.
sections.layout: Large typographic statement ('Ninety ways to bend a line.') followed by a macro image grid of distinct wire patterns.
sections.interaction: Tap a grid tile to isolate that motif full-bleed against a darkened backdrop with its pattern name, if known, and its use.

sections.title: What Silver Becomes
sections.purpose: Show the breadth of Tarakasi beyond jewellery: the full materials_and_forms list.
sections.layout: Asymmetrical catalogue gallery (editorial masonry, not a uniform card grid).
sections.rule: Use only real, licensed photographs. Never generate replacement artefacts that could be mistaken for authentic Tarakasi — this is a hard rule, not a style preference.

sections.title: Silver in Motion
sections.purpose: Explain Tarakasi's role as the traditional ornament set of Odissi dance, head to waist.
sections.layout: Full-height editorial image of an Odissi dancer's ornament set with labelled zones (see content_inventory.odissi.named_forms).
sections.interaction: Tap/hover labels to identify each named ornament form and its body zone — behaves like an interactive museum object label, not a shopping tag.

sections.title: When Cuttack Turns Silver
sections.purpose: Tell the Chandi Medha story: the 16th-century Sharadiya Utsav root, 150+ artisans working annually, and the dated history of specific backdrops growing from 250 kg to 500 kg+.
sections.layout: Large photographic panorama of a Chandi Medha backdrop, with a detail inset showing individual wirework up close.
sections.data_visual: A minimal, typographic weight-timeline (1956 → 250kg, 1991 → 350kg, 2004 → 483kg, 2005 → 500kg, 2006 → 450kg) rendered as a restrained bar-rule chart in silver tones — not a flashy infographic.
sections.interaction: Pinch/drag zoom on the panorama image, desktop and mobile alike.

sections.title: Made in Cuttack
sections.purpose: Connect the craft to the city's identity as a historic trading hub and the 'Silver City' epithet.
sections.layout: Minimal city section — a short editorial paragraph, one strong photograph, and a small labelled note of the three named craft neighbourhoods (Nayasadak, Balu Bazaar, Mangalabag). No generic tourism map interface.
sections.content: Use only Cuttack-related description present in content_inventory.cuttack.

sections.title: A Name Protected by Place
sections.purpose: Explain the 2024 GI recognition and what it legally means.
sections.visual: Quiet, typographic seal-like treatment built from type and a hairline circle rule — explicitly not a fake government emblem or official-looking crest.
sections.interaction: Simple expandable explainer: date, definition, regulator, 10-year protection term, sibling GI crafts named the same period.

sections.title: The Craft Must Continue
sections.purpose: Address the survival challenge with dignity, specificity, and an ending on continuity rather than loss.
sections.layout: Dark editorial section (charcoal ground, silver_light type), restrained photography of real tools/workshop interiors — no pity imagery, no artisan portraits without explicit rights.
themes: ~400 artisans currently estimated working in Cuttack
renewed interest via fashion/exhibition and training centres
sections.closing_beat: End this section, and by extension the site's difficult content, on the oaklores note about renewed design interest and training support — the craft's continuation, not its endangerment, is the last word.

sections.title: The Thread Continues
sections.purpose: End on the craft itself, not a generic call-to-action.
sections.visual: One slowly moving macro shot of a finished piece catching natural light — can echo/loop back to the hero shot to close the circle.

sections.title: Sources & Further Reading
sections.purpose: Transparent attribution and editorial provenance — this is a load-bearing trust section for a heritage site, not a footnote.
sections.layout: Clean bibliography: six entries, each with publication/site name, article title, direct URL, and role played in the site's content (pull from source_policy.source_keys[*].role).

visual_system.art_direction: Contemporary museum catalogue meets intimate craft documentary. Think: a beautifully typeset exhibition catalogue for a serious jewellery/metalwork museum show, shot through with the slow patience of a craft documentary film.
reference_mood: Cooper Hewitt / V&A digital exhibition microsites
Aesop's editorial restraint (without becoming a beauty-brand pastiche)
Japanese craft documentaries — long static macro shots, natural light, silence
Physical jewellery-house lookbooks that photograph the object, not a model wearing it
visual_system.palette_rule: Silver is represented through photography, real material texture, and tonal/value contrast — never a fake CSS metallic gradient. The warm_accent is used sparingly (a single word, a rule, a small numeral) — never as a dominant brand colour, since the subject is silver, not gold.

typography.display: An elegant, high-contrast serif (e.g. a Didone or transitional serif such as Canela, Reckless, or GT Sectra) for titles and section headers. If multilingual (Odia) support is added later, pair with a serif offering solid Odia-script metrics rather than a mismatched system fallback.
typography.body: A neutral humanist sans-serif with excellent readability at small sizes (e.g. Inter, Untitled Sans, or GT America) for editorial copy.
typography.micro: A restrained sans or monospace (e.g. a light-weight grotesk or a quiet mono like GT America Mono) for process labels, source citations, timeline dates and metadata — signals 'documentation', separate from the editorial voice.
typography.scale_note: Large typography is used to slow the reader down at key moments (hero title, wire_language statement), but never becomes decoration for its own sake — every oversized line must carry real content.
typography.line_height: 1.5 for body copy at reading_width; 1.1–1.2 for display type.

allowed: real metal texture from photography only
forbidden: generic mandala/paisley/lotus motifs used as decoration

layout.asymmetry_rule: Object/gallery and history sections should break the grid deliberately (off-center images, uneven column spans) — the 12-col grid is a discipline to break with intent, not a rule to follow uniformly on every section.

imagery_direction.photography_style: Macro-first. Shallow depth of field, single directional light source (mimics workshop lamp/window light), true-to-material silver tone — not warmed/goldened in post. Avoid flat product-catalogue lighting for hero/section-opener images; reserve flat even lighting only for the museum-catalogue object shots in 'objects' and 'odissi'.
imagery_direction.people_policy: No AI-generated or stock 'artisan' faces. If real, rights-cleared artisan photography becomes available, treat hands-at-work shots (mid-process, tools visible) as strongly preferred over posed portraits.
imagery_direction.scale_device: Recurring visual device across the site: extreme close-up of wire juxtaposed with a wide shot of a massive Chandi Medha — repeat this scale contrast at least twice (making section, durga_puja section) to reinforce the site's core visual idea.

motion_system.principle: Motion should feel like handling a delicate object: slow, precise, almost physical — as though the interface itself could be dented if moved carelessly.
motion_system.signature_motion: The 'wire line' motif: a single SVG path that draws/bends/coils in sync with scroll position, used in the hero-to-opening transition and throughout the making section. This is the site's one recurring, ownable motion signature — do not introduce a second competing signature effect elsewhere.
allowed: slow image scale from 1.03 to 1.00 on load/reveal
mask reveals (image revealed via an expanding shape, not a wipe gimmick)
SVG line-drawing (stroke-dashoffset) for the wire motif
gentle parallax under 30px on hero imagery only
micro hover brightness/contrast shift (±4–6%) on interactive tiles
magnifier/loupe reveal on hover or tap for macro detail insets
forbidden: constant/idle floating or breathing animation on static elements
parallax layers that hurt mobile scroll performance
motion_system.reduced_motion: Respect prefers-reduced-motion fully: replace all scroll choreography (wire line, parallax, mask reveals) with simple opacity fades; the ProcessStepper must remain fully legible as a static vertical list with no animation dependency.

mobile_rules: Mobile is designed as a first-class editorial experience, not a collapsed desktop layout.
Hero is capped at 72–88vh and never places text over busy image detail — use a scrim or a quieter crop instead of lowering text contrast.
All split (text/image) layouts stack, image-to-text rhythm deliberately alternated section to section so the page doesn't feel monotonous.
No horizontal carousel as the sole way to reach content — gallery/catalogue sections must remain fully reachable via vertical scroll.
The making-section wire animation becomes a vertical stepper with scroll-snap between steps.
Large images use true responsive crops (art-directed per breakpoint), not a shrunk desktop image.
Navigation collapses to a full-screen or bottom-sheet menu with large touch-friendly section links.
Source notes stay inline and readable at mobile width — never hidden behind a hover-only tooltip.
No essential information is hover-only; every interactive reveal (loupe, labels, expandable GI explainer) has a tap-equivalent.

component_system.card_rule: Cards are used only where they genuinely improve information grouping (e.g. the GI sibling-crafts note, the workshop-realities aside). Default to editorial compositions, image-led layouts and open space rather than boxed cards.

media_and_asset_manifest.principle: Build a separate structured image manifest before development starts — this design file specifies its shape, not its content, since actual photography/licensing is the client's responsibility.
manifest_fields: source_key (if drawn from a cited source's context)
media_and_asset_manifest.placeholder_policy: Until real, licensed photography is supplied, use clearly-labelled grey/silver placeholder blocks with a text note of the intended shot (e.g. 'MACRO — wire being twisted, directional light') rather than AI-generated stand-in imagery — a placeholder must never be mistaken for a real artefact.

Making: one photo per process step (11 shots)
Wire language: 6–10 distinct wire-pattern macro tiles
Objects: minimum 2 photos per category (12+ total)
Durga Puja: one panorama Chandi Medha shot + one macro detail inset
Challenge: 2–3 workshop/tool interior shots (no posed portraits without explicit rights)

requirements: full keyboard navigation, including the wire-line scroll animation and expandable GI explainer
semantic heading hierarchy (single h1 in hero, h2 per section)
descriptive alt text for every meaningful image, referencing the manifest's alt_text field
decorative imagery marked aria-hidden / empty alt
sufficient text contrast, including silver_mid/silver_dark text-on-background combinations checked against AA
no information conveyed by colour alone (timeline eras, GI status use icon/text, not colour coding)

targets: responsive WebP/AVIF imagery with defined crop variants
avoid autoplay video on mobile unless extremely lightweight (<2MB, muted, short loop) and user-controllable
keep all animation GPU-friendly (transform/opacity only, avoid layout-triggering properties)
prefer CSS/Web Animations API over large animation libraries; a scroll-linked library is acceptable only for the wire-line motif if CSS scroll-timeline support is insufficient
target excellent Core Web Vitals (LCP < 2.5s, CLS < 0.1, INP < 200ms) on a mid-tier mobile device profile

seo_and_metadata.title: Tarakasi — The Silver Filigree of Cuttack
seo_and_metadata.description: Explore Cuttack Rupa Tarakasi: its many-accounted history, the silver-wire making process, its motifs, its role in Odissi and Durga Puja, its 2024 GI recognition, and the challenges facing this living craft today.
seo_and_metadata.rule: Do not add unsupported historical dates or claims to metadata or structured data that are not already present in content_inventory.

anti_slop_checklist: No generic 'Discover the beauty of India' copy.
No fake poetic claims not grounded in the supplied sources.

No invented artisan names or quotes (Jagdish Mishra, the one named artisan in the Wikipedia source, may be referenced only if his quoted material is reproduced accurately and attributed — do not invent additional dialogue for him).
No invented statistics beyond those explicitly sourced (500+ years, 90% silver, 90 wire types, ~400 artisans, 150+ puja artisans, specific Chandi Medha weights/years, 15 March 2024 GI date).
No generic lotus/mandala decoration just because the subject is Indian.
No gold-heavy luxury-brand treatment — the subject is silver; warm_accent stays a minor note, not a dominant hue.
No excessive rounded rectangles / bubbly card UI.
No decorative animation that competes with or upstages the filigree photography.
No fake museum labels pretending to be historical records — the HistoryTimeline must always show its source attribution, never present as an unsourced 'fact plaque'.
No single definitive origin story when the supplied sources themselves qualify or disagree on the origin — see origin_and_history.design.
No fake GI seal/emblem styled to resemble an official government mark.

implementation_notes.preferred_stack: Any modern React/Next.js (or equivalent) stack; semantic HTML, CSS-first animation, progressive enhancement so content reads without JS.
implementation_notes.image_strategy: Build the image manifest (see media_and_asset_manifest) before component work starts — asset id, source key, licence status, crop variants, alt text, focal point.
implementation_notes.content_model: Keep all editorial copy, including source tags, in structured JSON/MDX (mirroring content_inventory's shape) rather than hard-coding paragraphs into components — this keeps the source-attribution system enforceable and editable.
implementation_notes.animation_architecture: IntersectionObserver / CSS scroll-timeline for reveals; a dedicated SVG path-animation module for the wire-line signature motif, driven by scroll progress and gracefully degrading to a static image under reduced-motion.
implementation_notes.mobile_testing: Test at 320, 360, 390, 412 and 430px widths plus tablet portrait/landscape, focusing especially on the ProcessStepper vertical-stepper mode and the FestivalScaleViewer pinch-zoom.
implementation_notes.pre_launch_editorial_task: A human editor must re-verify the Vikaspedia source's exact wording live (see source_policy.source_keys.vikaspedia.note_to_developer) before the History section ships, since that page did not fully render during this design pass.
implementation_notes.quality_bar: The final result should read as a digital exhibition or premium cultural publication — closer to a museum microsite than a template-based business/portfolio site. If in doubt on any design decision, choose the option that removes an element rather than adds one.
